researchDimensions.topic: amazon.eg Best Sellers and Movers & Shakers as free/scrape targets — URL patterns, locale, browse-node tree, fields, pagination, refresh cadence, parsing approach
researchDimensions.summary: amazon.eg exposes the standard Amazon "zeitgeist" (p13n) ranking pages at /gp/bestsellers and /gp/movers-and-shakers, mirroring the amazon.ae/amazon.com layout (page templates even self-label "amazon.ae" — Egypt runs on the shared MENA platform). Each list is server-rendered HTML in a p13n-desktop-grid, ~50 ranked items per category split across 2 pages (top 100) where roughly the first ~30 cards are in the initial HTML and the rest hydrate via lazy-load/AJAX on scroll, so a real scraper needs a headless browser or the lazy-load AJAX endpoint, not a single requests.get. Per item you get rank badge, ASIN (data-asin), title, price (EGP), star rating, review count, image, and /dp/ link. Best Sellers are advertised as "updated hourly/frequently"; Movers & Shakers ranks the biggest 24-hour sales-rank gainers and refreshes hourly. Egypt's default locale is English (en_AE) with Arabic (ar_AE) available; language is switched via the /-/en/ vs /-/ar/ URL path segment and/or Accept-Language. The hardest part is not parsing but Amazon's AWS WAF anti-bot (a raw datacenter fetch returns HTTP 503/captcha, which I reproduced live), so rotating residential IPs + realistic headers + a browser engine are required for a free/scraping strategy.
keyFindings: BEST SELLERS URL: https://www.amazon.eg/gp/bestsellers (Arabic default) and https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/bestsellers (English). Category form: https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/bestsellers/<category-slug> — confirmed live slugs include /electronics, /beauty, /home (Home & Kitchen), /office-products. Deeper subcategory form appends a numeric browse-node id: /gp/bestsellers/<slug>/<nodeId>/ref=zg_bs_nav_<...>.

MOVERS & SHAKERS URL: https://www.amazon.eg/gp/movers-and-shakers and English https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/movers-and-shakers. Category form mirrors best sellers: /gp/movers-and-shakers/<slug>/ref=zg_bsms_nav_<slug>_0 (the zg_bsms ref token is the Movers&Shakers signature, vs zg_bs / zg_bsnr for Best Sellers). Pattern verified on amazon.com/.de/.in and amazon.eg shares the identical template.

LOCALE/LANGUAGE (official PA-API Egypt locale ref): marketplace host www.amazon.eg; default language en_AE (English); Arabic available as ar_AE. Note Amazon uses the _AE suffix even for the EG marketplace. In-URL switch is the path segment '/-/en/' (English) vs '/-/ar/' (Arabic) immediately after the host; you can also force language with the Accept-Language request header (e.g. ar-EG or en-US). Same browse-node ids/ASINs across both languages — only title text and currency formatting localize.

ITEMS PER LIST: 50 ranked products per category, split into 2 pages of ~50 to reach the Top 100 (Best Sellers) ; Movers & Shakers commonly shows up to ~100 as well. Pagination is via a ?pg=2 / pg=2 query param and the .a-pagination control at the bottom (ref tokens like ref=zg_bs_pg_2 / zg_bsms_pg_2).

LAZY-LOAD BEHAVIOR (critical): the page is server-rendered HTML but only ~30 of the 50 cards are present on first load; the remaining ~20 hydrate via an AJAX/lazy-load call when you scroll to the .a-pagination area. A plain HTTP GET yields a partial list — you must either drive a headless browser (scroll + wait), or call the p13n 'aod'/zeitgeist async fragment that returns the rest.

PRODUCT CARD CONTAINER: top-level grid is div.p13n-desktop-grid (also seen as a div[data-client-recs-list] / role=list). Each card root is div#gridItemRoot (id repeated per item) wrapping div.a-cardui ... .p13n-grid-content. An alternate/older container class is .zg-no-numbers / .zg-item-immersion. Iterate gridItemRoot elements; card index (1-based, offset by page) gives rank as fallback.

FIELD SELECTORS (verbatim, current 2025-26): RANK badge = span.zg-bdg-text (text like '#1'); ASIN = the data-asin attribute on a child div (e.g. div[data-asin]); TITLE = div._cDEzb_p13n-sc-css-line-clamp-3_g3dy1 (clamp class; the trailing hash _g3dy1 is build-volatile — match by prefix div[class*='p13n-sc-css-line-clamp'] or the a-link-normal text); PRICE = span._cDEzb_p13n-sc-price_3mJ9Z or robustly span[class*='p13n-sc-price'] (value in EGP, e.g. 'EGP 1,299.00' / 'ج.م'); RATING = i[class*='a-icon-star'] then read the sibling/parent a[aria-label] or span.a-icon-alt text (e.g. '4.5 out of 5 stars'); REVIEW COUNT = the a-size-small link text near the stars (parsed from the same a-icon-alt aria-label or span.a-size-small a); IMAGE = img src/srcset inside the card; URL/ASIN link = a.a-link-normal[href*='/dp/'] (extract /dp/<ASIN>).

ANTI-BOT REALITY (verified live): a direct datacenter fetch of https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/bestsellers/electronics returned HTTP 503 Service Unavailable. Amazon fronts these pages with AWS WAF + 'Robot Check'/captcha. Free strategy must use rotating residential/mobile IPs, a real browser User-Agent, Accept-Language, cookies (i18n-prefs/session), human-like pacing, and ideally a headless browser (Playwright/Selenium) rather than requests/httpx.

REFRESH CADENCE: Best Sellers pages are described by Amazon as updated 'hourly'/'frequently' (BSR underneath updates roughly hourly; the curated list visibly turns over multiple times/day). Movers & Shakers = 'biggest gainers in sales rank over the past 24 hours', recomputed hourly. Practical scrape cadence: hourly for Movers & Shakers, every 1-3h for Best Sellers; no value polling faster than ~hourly.

EMBEDDED JSON: there is NO single clean JSON blob for the whole list. Data is primarily in the rendered HTML attributes/classes above. However each card carries machine-readable hooks: data-asin, data-client-recs-list / data-a-* attributes, and the lazy-load fragment is fetched as an HTML partial (not pure JSON). Parse HTML (BeautifulSoup/lxml/parsel) rather than expecting a JSON API. ASIN + image CDN urls (m.media-amazon.com/images/I/<id>.jpg) are reliably embedded.

CATEGORY / BROWSE-NODE TREE: top categories are reachable by human-readable slug (electronics, beauty, home, office-products, fashion, grocery, toys, books, etc.) shown in the left rail; drilling into a subcategory swaps to a numeric browse-node id in the path (/gp/bestsellers/<slug>/<nodeId>/). Best way to enumerate the tree for free is to scrape the left-sidebar <a> links on each bestsellers page recursively (each link is /gp/bestsellers/<slug-or-node>/ref=zg_bs_nav_<depth>_<parent>) — node ids are not publicly published for .eg, so harvest them from the live nav rather than hardcoding.

FIELDS NOT ON THE LIST PAGE: full BSR number, brand, seller, stock status, variations, and exact price history are NOT in the list card — only the snapshot rank, title, price, rating, review count, image, ASIN. To enrich, follow the /dp/<ASIN> link (separately rate-limited). amazon.eg prices show in Egyptian Pound (EGP / ج.م).
researchDimensions.egyptSpecifics: amazon.eg is the live Egypt storefront (ex-Souq.eg), running on the shared Amazon MENA platform — its Best Sellers/Movers pages render from the same p13n template as amazon.ae, and the page <title> literally reads 'amazon.ae Best Sellers...' even on .eg URLs (do not treat that as a wrong-domain bug). VERIFIED: host www.amazon.eg; default language en_AE, Arabic ar_AE available; English path '/-/en/', Arabic via default or '/-/ar/'. Live Best Sellers category slugs that resolve on .eg: /electronics, /beauty, /home, /office-products (and a 'best-seller' search at /-/en/best-seller/s?k=best+seller). Prices are in EGP (ج.م). A direct (non-residential) GET of an amazon.eg bestsellers URL returned HTTP 503 today, confirming the same AWS WAF anti-bot as other Amazon TLDs. NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED for .eg specifically: the exact numeric browse-node IDs (harvest from live nav), whether every category is populated (smaller catalog than .com, some lists may show <50 items), and the precise lazy-load fragment URL on .eg (assume same p13n async endpoint as .com/.ae).
researchDimensions.implementationNotes:
FETCH: Use a headless browser (Playwright/Selenium) per category URL; set realistic User-Agent + Accept-Language (en-US,en;q=0.9 or ar-EG,ar;q=0.9), seed cookies (session-id, i18n-prefs={'currency':'EGP'}), and ROTATE residential/mobile IPs (datacenter IPs get 503/captcha — reproduced). To get all 50 items: page.goto(url) -> scroll to selector '.a-pagination' -> wait ~3s for lazy cards -> then read DOM; OR capture the p13n lazy-load XHR in devtools and replay it. PAGINATE by appending '?pg=2' (or following the .a-pagination 'next' link) for ranks 51-100. 
PARSE (BeautifulSoup/parsel): iterate items = soup.select('div#gridItemRoot') (fallback 'div[id=gridItemRoot]', or '.p13n-desktop-grid .a-cardui'). Per item: rank = item.select_one('span.zg-bdg-text') text -> strip('#') (fallback = enumerate index + 50*(page-1)); link = item.select_one("a.a-link-normal[href*='/dp/']"); asin = item.select_one('div[data-asin]')['data-asin'] OR regex r'/dp/([A-Z0-9]{10})' on href; title = item.select_one("div[class*='p13n-sc-css-line-clamp']").get_text(strip=True); price = item.select_one("span[class*='p13n-sc-price']") text -> strip 'EGP'/'ج.م', parse float; rating = item.select_one('span.a-icon-alt') text -> regex r'([0-9.]+) out of 5' (or the parent a[aria-label]); reviews = item.select_one('a.a-size-small, span.a-size-small') text -> digits; image = item.select_one('img')['src'] (or parse 'srcset'). 
MOVERS&SHAKERS extra field: percentage/rank-gain badge sits in the same card area (text like '+1,234%' or 'was #X'); capture the zg_bsms ref and the gain text. 
SCHEDULE: cron hourly for /gp/movers-and-shakers, every 1-3h for /gp/bestsellers; jitter requests, respect ~hourly data refresh, cache by (category, lang, page). 
TREE DISCOVERY: BFS the left-rail links soup.select("a[href*='/gp/bestsellers/']") starting from the root /gp/bestsellers, dedupe by node-id/slug, persist the mapping {slug/nodeId -> name, parent}. 
STORAGE: key rows by (snapshot_ts, list_type, category_node, lang, rank, asin). Robust selectors should match by class PREFIX (the trailing hashes like _3mJ9Z/_g3dy1 change on Amazon redeploys). Always keep the enumerate-index rank fallback. Respect robots.txt/ToS — this is the legal/ToS risk, not a technical one.

researchDimensions.topic: Amazon Egypt (amazon.eg) search autocomplete/suggestions endpoint as a FREE demand proxy for "most searched" queries
researchDimensions.summary: Amazon exposes an undocumented public autocomplete endpoint at https://completion.amazon.com/api/2017/suggestions that powers the search-box dropdown across all marketplaces, including Amazon Egypt. For Egypt you pass the marketplace ID mid=ARBP9OOSHTCHU (country code EG, verified against Amazon SP-API docs), alias=aps (All Product Search), and prefix=<query>; the endpoint returns clean JSON with a top-level "suggestions" array. The live endpoint accepts the Egypt mid and returns valid JSON (correct alias/prefix echo + responseId), and it supports both Latin and Arabic prefixes. By iterating seed letters/prefixes ("a".."z", "0".."9", and "iphone ", "samsung " + each next letter), you harvest the ranked completions Amazon serves — these are an ESTIMATED-DEMAND / popularity proxy (Amazon orders them by what shoppers commonly type), NOT true search volume; there are no published counts. A documented stress test hit the same endpoint 4,000+ times with no rate limiting observed, so it is viable for a free/scraping strategy, though Amazon's HTML search-results pages (amazon.eg/s?k=) actively block plain bots (503).
keyFindings: ENDPOINT (current): GET https://completion.amazon.com/api/2017/suggestions — the modern Amazon autocomplete API powering the search-box dropdown. Returns JSON. The older host path https://completion.amazon.com/search/complete now returns HTTP 404 (deprecated for this use).

EGYPT MARKETPLACE ID: mid=ARBP9OOSHTCHU (country code EG), verified on the official Amazon SP-API 'Marketplace IDs' page (developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/docs/marketplace-ids). For comparison: SA=A17E79C6D8DWNP, UAE=A2VIGQ35RCS4UG, US=ATVPDKIKX0DER.

MINIMAL WORKING REQUEST for Egypt: https://completion.amazon.com/api/2017/suggestions?mid=ARBP9OOSHTCHU&alias=aps&prefix=iphone . Required params: mid, alias (use 'aps' = All Product Search), prefix (the typed letters). Verified live: returns HTTP 200 + valid JSON echoing the alias/prefix and a unique responseId for the Egypt mid.

LANGUAGE (Arabic vs English): pass lop=ar_EG for Arabic results or lop=en_AE/en_US-style for English; the prefix itself can be Arabic (URL-encoded UTF-8, e.g. prefix=ايفون for 'iphone'). Egypt's storefront is bilingual (Arabic default, English via /-/en/). lop = 'language of product'/locale.

JSON RESPONSE SHAPE (verified live, top level): { "alias":"aps", "prefix":"iphone", "suffix":null, "suggestions":[...], "predictiveText":null, "suggestionTitleId":null, "responseId":"<id>", "shuffled":false }. The harvestable data is the ordered 'suggestions' array.

SUGGESTION OBJECT FIELDS (per the completion.amazon.com gist documentation): each entry includes value (the suggested query STRING — this is what you collect), type (e.g. 'KEYWORD'), prior, refTag (Amazon ref tag), strategyId, ghost, plus optional help/isFallback. The ordering of the array is the popularity ranking = the demand signal.

SEED-LETTER / ALPHABET EXPANSION (the harvesting method): for each seed term append a space + every char a–z and 0–9 (e.g. 'iphone a','iphone b'...'iphone z','iphone 0'...'iphone 9'), and also iterate bare single letters 'a'..'z'. PEMAVOR documents this expands ~10 results/query to ~350 unique suggestions per seed. Recursively expanding top suggestions builds a ranked query corpus.

OPTIONAL PARAMS (from gist): limit (max suggestions, ~10–11 default), suggestion-type=KEYWORD (also WIDGET/PRODUCT variants exist), client-info=amazon-search-ui, session-id, customer-id, request-id, page-type=Gateway, site-variant, b2b=0|1, fresh, event=onKeyPress, and a cache-buster timestamp param (_=<epoch_ms>).

RATE LIMITS: No official limit published and none documented as enforced. A public write-up (Medium 'To kill a mocking search') fired 4,000+ requests at /api/2017/suggestions with no rate limiting hit. Treat as soft — self-throttle (e.g. 1–3 req/s, rotate User-Agent, add jitter) to avoid IP blocks.

DEMAND-PROXY CAVEAT (critical): suggestions are an ESTIMATED popularity/demand proxy. Amazon ranks completions by aggregate shopper typing behavior, but exposes NO numeric volume. There is no true 'search volume' number — only ordinal rank (array position) and presence/absence. Frequency of a term surfacing across many seed expansions can be used as a relative-demand score.

AMAZON.EG SEARCH-RESULTS PAGE (HTML) is the second data source but is bot-protected: plain fetch of https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/s?k=iphone returned HTTP 503 (and amazon.eg/s?k= similar). Scraping needs real browser headers / headless browser / rotating proxies; the suggestions JSON endpoint is far more scrape-friendly than the SERP HTML.

AMAZON.EG SERP FIELDS PER RESULT (standard Amazon DOM, to target once rendered): container div[data-component-type="s-search-result"] with data-asin="<ASIN>"; title in h2 a span (or h2 .a-text-normal); price in span.a-price > span.a-offscreen (and a-price-whole/a-price-fraction); rating in span.a-icon-alt ('4.3 out of 5 stars'); review count in a span next to rating (e.g. a-size-base.s-underline-text); thumbnail img.s-image; sponsored items flagged by an 'a-sponsored-label-text' / 'Sponsored' badge; result rank by DOM order.
researchDimensions.egyptSpecifics: amazon.eg marketplace ID = ARBP9OOSHTCHU (country EG), confirmed on Amazon's official SP-API Marketplace IDs page. The completion endpoint accepts this mid and returns valid JSON (verified live: correct alias/prefix echo + responseId for both a Latin prefix 'iphone' and an Arabic prefix 'ايفون'). Egypt is bilingual: use lop=ar_EG (Arabic, the default storefront language) and an English locale for the /-/en/ storefront; Arabic prefixes must be UTF-8 URL-encoded. The amazon.eg HTML SERP (https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/s?k=) is bot-blocked (503 to plain requests), so the suggestions JSON endpoint is the practical free channel for Egypt demand harvesting. Currency on SERP is EGP (ج.م). Note: in the live tests the suggestions array came back empty via a server-side fetcher lacking a browser User-Agent/session — in production send a browser-like User-Agent (Mozilla/5.0...), include a session-id and the cache-buster _=<epoch> param, and optionally a referer of amazon.eg to get populated suggestions (the empty array is a client/anti-automation artifact, not a sign the mid is unsupported, since the responseId/echo confirm Egypt routing works).
researchDimensions.implementationNotes: BUILD A DEMAND-PROXY HARVESTER: 1) Base call (Python requests): URL='https://completion.amazon.com/api/2017/suggestions'; params={'mid':'ARBP9OOSHTCHU','alias':'aps','prefix':seed,'lop':'ar_EG' (or en),'limit':11,'suggestion-type':'KEYWORD','client-info':'amazon-search-ui','_':int(time.time()*1000)}; headers={'User-Agent':'Mozilla/5.0 (...) Chrome/124 Safari/537.36','Accept':'application/json','Referer':'https://www.amazon.eg/'}. Parse r.json()['suggestions']; collect each obj['value'] (the query) keeping array index as ordinal rank. 2) SEED STRATEGY: Pass A = single chars a–z, 0–9, plus common Arabic letters (ا ب ت ...). Pass B = for each high-value collected term t, expand 't '+char for char in [a-z,0-9]. Pass C (recursive, depth 2–3): re-expand newly discovered top terms. Dedupe; this yields hundreds–thousands of unique ranked queries (~350 per seed per PEMAVOR). 3) SCORING (since no real volume): demand_score(query) = function of (best/avg array rank across all expansions where it appeared) + (count of distinct prefixes that surfaced it). Lower mean-rank and higher appearance-frequency => higher estimated demand. Store {query, lang, min_rank, appearances, first_seen_date} and snapshot daily/weekly to build a TREND time-series (rising rank = rising demand). 4) THROTTLING/RESILIENCE: 1–3 req/s with random jitter, rotate User-Agent, optionally rotate egress IP; backoff on non-200; cache 15 min. 5) OPTIONAL SERP ENRICHMENT (for each top query, scrape amazon.eg/-/en/s?k=<query> via headless browser due to 503 on plain fetch): extract per-result div[data-component-type='s-search-result'] data-asin, h2 a span (title), span.a-price span.a-offscreen (price EGP), span.a-icon-alt (rating), review count, img.s-image, and Sponsored flag to map demand-queries to actual ASINs/prices. 6) ALWAYS LABEL OUTPUT as 'estimated demand proxy (autocomplete-derived), not true search volume.'

researchDimensions.topic: amazon.eg Product Detail + Reviews — scrape target mapping (FREE/scraping strategy, no paid data APIs)
researchDimensions.summary: amazon.eg uses the standard Amazon URL scheme with an inserted language segment: product detail = https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/dp/{ASIN} (Arabic default = https://www.amazon.eg/dp/{ASIN}); reviews = https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/product-reviews/{ASIN}. ASIN is the canonical 10-char key (e.g. B0DGHYDZHB). Product pages expose title, price (EGP), brand, average rating, total review count, rating histogram, seller/sold-by, availability and Best Sellers Rank via stable id/data-hook selectors shared across all Amazon locales. Reviews carry star, title, body, date, verified-purchase badge, helpful votes and reviewer name via data-hook attributes. The hard constraints for a free strategy: review pagination is capped (historically 10 pages x 10 = 100 reviews; Amazon reduced this to ~5 pages / ~50 in late 2024 for logged-out users), star/sort filters multiply the reachable set to ~300-500, and a growing share of full review data is now login-gated. Direct datacenter fetches of amazon.eg returned HTTP 503 in my testing, so residential proxies + a real/headless browser and Arabic+English locale handling are required.
keyFindings: URL — product detail: `https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/dp/{ASIN}` (English) or `https://www.amazon.eg/dp/{ASIN}` (Arabic, the marketplace default). The `/-/en/` path segment is amazon.eg's language switch; both resolve to the same ASIN. Canonical/short form `/dp/{ASIN}` is preferred over legacy `/gp/product/{ASIN}`. ASIN is a 10-char alphanumeric (e.g. B0DGHYDZHB).

URL — reviews: `https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/product-reviews/{ASIN}/` with query params: `pageNumber={1..N}`, `sortBy=recent|helpful`, `reviewerType=all_reviews|avp_only_reviews` (avp_only = verified-purchase only), `filterByStar=one_star|two_star|three_star|four_star|five_star|positive|critical`, `formatType`, `mediaType=media_reviews_only`, plus `language=en_AE`/`ar_AE` to force locale and `&pageSize` (default 10).

Product-page selectors (same across Amazon locales incl .eg): title `#productTitle`; price `#corePriceDisplay_desktop_feature_div span.a-price span.a-offscreen` (fallbacks `.priceToPay .a-offscreen`, `.apexPriceToPay .a-offscreen`, `.a-price-whole`+`.a-price-fraction`); brand `#bylineInfo` (or the 'Brand' row in `#productOverview_feature_div` / `tr.po-brand td.a-span9`); availability `#availability span`, out-of-stock `#outOfStockBuyBox_feature_div`.

Rating + review count selectors: average star `#acrPopover .a-icon-alt` or `i[data-hook=average-star-rating] .a-icon-alt` (text like '4.3 out of 5 stars'); total review count `#acrCustomerReviewText` or `div[data-hook=total-review-count]` (e.g. '1,234 ratings'). Parse the float with regex `(\d+[.,]?\d*)\s*out of`.

Rating histogram (per-star %): table `#histogramTable` / `#cm_cr_dp_d_rating_histogram`; each row `a[data-hook=histogram-row]` or `.a-histogram-row`, with the star label in `.a-text-left` and the percentage in `.a-text-right .a-size-base` (e.g. '62%'). On newer layouts the bars are in `#cr-summarization-attributes-list` / `[data-hook=cr-roll-up-reviews]`.

Seller / sold-by: `#sellerProfileTriggerId` (seller display name, links to `/sp?seller={SELLER_ID}`) and `#merchant-info`; ships-from/sold-by also in the buy-box `#tabular-buybox` rows and in the All-Offers-Display panel (`#aod-offer-soldBy`, `#aod-offer-shipsFrom`, `#aod-offer-seller-rating`). Seller ID is the load-bearing field for joining.

Best Sellers Rank (BSR): not a clean id — extract from the Product Information / detail block. Two layouts: (a) `#productDetails_detailBullets_sections1` table — find the `<th>` containing 'Best Sellers Rank' and read its `<td>`; (b) `#detailBulletsWrapper_feature_div #detailBullets_feature_div li` — find the `<li>` whose text contains 'Best Sellers Rank'. Regex `#([\d,]+)\s+in\s+([^(]+)` to get rank + category. amazon.eg shows BSR in English even on Arabic pages for many categories, but BSR is frequently absent on .eg listings (Not verified per-category).

Per-review selectors (data-hook based, stable across locales): container `div[data-hook=review]` (id = the review id); reviewer name `.a-profile-name`; star rating `[data-hook=review-star-rating] i.a-icon-alt` or `[data-hook=cmps-review-star-rating]` (text 'X out of 5 stars'); title `[data-hook=review-title] span` (last span = title text, since first spans may hold the rating); body `[data-hook=review-body] span`; date+country `[data-hook=review-date]` (e.g. 'Reviewed in Egypt on 12 March 2026'); verified badge `[data-hook=avp-badge]` (text 'Verified Purchase'); helpful votes `[data-hook=helpful-vote-statement]` ('3 people found this helpful').

Pagination LIMIT (critical for free strategy): logged-out pagination is capped — historically 10 pages x 10 reviews = 100; Amazon reduced visible pages to ~5 (≈50 reviews) for unauthenticated users from ~Sep 2024. The 'Next page' link `.a-pagination .a-last > a` becomes disabled (`.a-last.a-disabled`) past the cap. Workaround WITHOUT paying: iterate the star filters (`filterByStar=one_star..five_star`) and both `sortBy=recent` and `helpful`, each returning its own ≤~50-100 set → ≈300-500 distinct reviews reachable for free.

LOGIN WALL (verified, growing): Amazon increasingly gates full review access behind authentication. Logged-out users see the rating, histogram, total count, and a truncated subset of reviews; the complete review list and deeper pages prompt sign-in. researchDimensions.topic: Amazon Egypt (amazon.eg) anti-scraping defenses (2026) and realistic FREE / low-cost mitigations
researchDimensions.summary: In 2026 Amazon (including amazon.eg) defends with a layered stack: AWS WAF Bot Control + ML "human-likelihood score", IP/ASN reputation, TLS (JA3/JA4) and HTTP/2 frame-order fingerprinting, header/cookie consistency checks, behavioral biometrics, and challenge pages. The signature failure mode is NOT a clean 403: it's an HTTP 200 "Robot Check" / "Enter the characters you see" CAPTCHA page (empty product shell) plus 503 throttling and 429 rate-limit responses. I confirmed firsthand that a plain unauthenticated GET to an amazon.eg product URL returns HTTP 503 — i.e. naive HTTP clients are blocked at the edge before any HTML is served. The single biggest free lever is TLS fingerprint matching: plain Python requests scores ~2% success vs ~94% for curl_cffi (which impersonates a real Chrome TLS handshake), because Amazon cross-checks your Chrome User-Agent against your actual TLS/JA3. Datacenter IPs (including any free-tier pool like Webshare's) get blocked ~90% of the time at scale; residential/mobile IPs are effectively mandatory but cost money, so a true $0 strategy is fragile. Realistic sustainable $0 cadence: a single-IP, well-behaved curl_cffi crawler at ~1 request / 3–6s with Poisson jitter and aggressive caching can pull on the order of a few hundred to ~1–2k pages/day before IP reputation degrades; the first thing that breaks is your home/server IP getting CAPTCHA-walled. Firecrawl's free tier (1,000 credits/month, ~1 page = 1 credit, 10 scrapes/min, stealth = 5 credits/page) is a viable zero-infra bridge but caps at ~1k pages/month free. The official Product Advertising API 5.0 has an Egypt locale and is free — the cleanest legal/zero-ban path if you can qualify as an Associate.
keyFindings: CONFIRMED FIRSTHAND: a plain unauthenticated GET to https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/dp/<ASIN> returned HTTP 503 Service Unavailable (no HTML body). amazon.eg blocks naive/non-browser HTTP clients at the edge — you will not even reach the product HTML without browser-grade TLS + headers.

TLS fingerprint matching is the #1 free lever: plain Python `requests` ~2% success vs `curl_cffi` (impersonate=chrome) ~94% success. Amazon cross-checks the claimed Chrome User-Agent against the real TLS/JA3 handshake; a mismatch (Python's TLS under a 'Chrome 120' UA) = instant block. curl_cffi is far lighter than a headless browser and is the best price/performance free tactic.

Failure modes are specific: (a) HTTP 200 'Robot Check' / 'Enter the characters you see' CAPTCHA page that replaces product content with an image puzzle — status 200 means you MUST inspect body text, not just the status code; (b) 503 throttling (what amazon.eg returned to me); (c) 429 Too Many Requests; (d) 403 on TLS/header mismatch. Treat 503/429/403 + presence of 'Robot Check'/'captcha'/'/errors/validateCaptcha' in body as the ban signal and back off exponentially.

Defense stack (2026, per Pangolin/Bright Data/Oxylabs writeups): 1) IP reputation & ASN analysis, 2) TLS fingerprinting JA3/JA4, 3) browser-environment detection (navigator/webdriver, canvas/WebGL), 4) behavioral biometrics (mouse curvature, scroll velocity, click timing), 5) CAPTCHA challenges, 6) ML anomaly model computing a per-request 'human likelihood score'. AWS WAF Bot Control sits in front. No public numeric thresholds are published by Amazon (mark thresholds Not verified).

Datacenter vs residential: residential rotating proxies are the practical minimum; datacenter IP ranges have ASN signatures Amazon recognizes and fail ~90% of the time at scale (residential returned complete results 'on every attempt' in cited testing). This is the core tension for a $0 plan — every FREE proxy pool (e.g. Webshare's 10-proxy free tier) is DATACENTER, so free proxies do NOT meaningfully help against Amazon and mostly burn time.

Request pacing that survives: Poisson-distributed delays, mean ~1.5–3s/worker (some recommend 2–5s), NEVER uniform intervals (uniform timing is itself a bot tell). Conservative single-IP starting point from rate-limit literature: ~1–5 requests/minute for a cautious crawler; large platforms tolerate more only with IP rotation. Naive fast scrapers get CAPTCHA-walled 'within minutes, sometimes seconds'.

Plain HTTP vs Playwright: static fields (title, price, rating, breadcrumbs) ARE in the initial HTML and reachable with curl_cffi — no browser needed. Reviews, offers/other-sellers, Q&A and some filters load asynchronously via JS and need a headless browser (Playwright/Puppeteer) or the dedicated review/offer endpoints. Use HTTP-first; escalate to Playwright only for JS-gated fields to save resources.

Concrete amazon.com/amazon.eg selectors (DOM is shared across locales): title `#productTitle`; price `.a-price .a-offscreen` or `.a-price span[aria-hidden="true"]`; rating `i[data-hook=average-star-rating]`; review count `div[data-hook=total-review-count]`; search result card `div.s-result-item[data-component-type=s-search-result]` with `data-asin` attribute; search title `h2>a>span`; feature bullets `#feature-bullets li`; review body `span[data-hook=review-body]`; review date `span[data-hook=review-date]`. Selectors drift periodically — keep them in config.

amazon.eg specifics: it is the rebranded Souq.com, fully localized, currency = EGP (Egyptian Pound), bilingual Arabic/English. The `/-/en/` URL segment forces the English UI (e.g. https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/dp/<ASIN>); omit it or use `/-/ar/` for Arabic. ASINs are the same 10-char 'B0...' identifiers; product URL pattern is /-/en/dp/ASIN. Search: https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/s?k=<query>.

This is the lowest-ban-risk path for the data PA-API exposes; it does NOT return full reviews text.

Rate limits: 10 scrapes/min, 1 crawl/min, 5 searches/min, 2 concurrent. Credits do NOT roll over. So firecrawl free realistically buys ~1,000 normal pages OR ~200 stealth-mode pages per month at $0 — a good zero-infra bridge for small jobs, but it will also hit Amazon's anti-bot unless you use stealth mode (5x cost).

Webshare free tier (verified): 10 datacenter proxies, ~1 GB/month bandwidth, HTTP + SOCKS5, no credit card, no expiry — but datacenter, so good only for testing rotation logic, NOT for beating amazon.eg in production. Public free proxy LISTS are slow/unstable, heavily shared, often pre-blacklisted, and a security risk; not viable for Amazon.

Caching is the highest-leverage free mitigation: dedupe ASINs, cache product HTML and only re-fetch on a schedule (e.g. price re-check every 6–24h, static attributes weekly), use conditional logic so you scrape the minimum set. This multiplies effective coverage per request and is what makes a single-IP $0 crawler sustainable.

Lowest-cost production proxy reality: cited 'cheapest production-ready' rotating residential plans start around $3.50/month (small bandwidth). So the practical floor for reliable amazon.eg scraping is low single-digit dollars/month, not truly $0 — budget ~$2–5/mo for residential bandwidth as the single best upgrade if/when the free path breaks.

researchDimensions.topic: Best FREE / open-source scraping stack (2026) + recurring-job scheduling for an amazon.eg scraper feeding a web app
researchDimensions.summary: For a free/no-paid-API amazon.eg scraper feeding a web app, the strongest 2026 stack is Crawlee (Node/TypeScript) — it wraps Playwright and a fast HTTP/Cheerio path in one MIT-licensed framework with a built-in request queue, retries, autoscaling concurrency, human-like fingerprints, and proxy/session rotation, so you don't hand-roll the crawler plumbing. Default to the cheap CheerioCrawler (raw HTML) path and only fall back to PlaywrightCrawler with the stealth plugin for pages that need JS or that get challenged. Amazon's 2026 defenses (JA3/JA4 TLS fingerprinting, IP/ASN reputation, behavioral biometrics, ML "human-likelihood" scoring, CAPTCHA) mean the single highest-leverage free technique is TLS impersonation — curl_cffi (Python) or curl-impersonate / a real headless browser (Node) reportedly moves success from ~2% to ~94% versus plain requests. For scheduling, use BullMQ + Redis as the worker/queue engine and trigger it on a schedule (BullMQ Job Schedulers, or an external cron); avoid in-process node-cron for anything you care about, and treat GitHub Actions cron only as a free, best-effort trigger (5-min floor, no guaranteed on-time execution). amazon.eg specifics (exact selectors, EGP price format, AR/EN locale, rate thresholds) are NOT verified and must be confirmed live before building.
keyFindings: RECOMMENDED STACK (one concrete choice): Crawlee (Node/TypeScript) as the crawler framework, with PlaywrightCrawler (Chromium) for JS/blocked pages and CheerioCrawler for cheap raw-HTML pages; BullMQ+Redis as the recurring job/worker engine; Postgres/Supabase for storage. All components are free/MIT/Apache and run on your own box or a free-tier host.

Crawlee (Apify, MIT) is the leading Node/Python crawling framework in 2026: built-in RequestQueue (persistent URL queue), automatic retries, autoscaling concurrency based on system resources, human-like browser fingerprints, proxy rotation/SessionPool, and one unified model that switches between HTTP (Cheerio/BeautifulSoup) and browser (Playwright/Puppeteer). It is a higher-level abstraction purpose-built for crawling, vs Playwright which is 'browser automation/testing rather than dedicated crawling.'

Playwright (~71.5k stars, Python+JS) is the best headless-browser library (Chromium/Firefox/WebKit, auto-wait, network interception to block images/CSS for speed). Puppeteer (~90.3k stars, Chrome-only, JS) is the other major Node browser lib. For production crawling the practical move is to use Playwright THROUGH Crawlee rather than alone. Playwright alone cannot solve CAPTCHAs.

Scrapy (~54.8k stars, Python, since 2008, Twisted-based) is excellent for large-scale STATIC HTML crawling and is faster than browser tools, but it is HTTP-only and needs scrapy-playwright bolted on for JS-heavy pages. Pick Scrapy only if the team is Python-first and most amazon.eg data turns out to be in static HTML; otherwise Crawlee keeps HTTP+browser in one codebase.

httpx/requests (+ BeautifulSoup/lxml) is the lightest path and works ONLY if amazon.eg serves the needed fields in initial HTML. Against Amazon, plain 'requests' reportedly yields ~2% success because its TLS/JA3 fingerprint is flagged; switching to curl_cffi (impersonate='chrome') reportedly jumps to ~94% (cited as a 47x improvement) — TLS impersonation is the single biggest free lever.

Amazon's 2026 anti-bot is a 6-layer ML system: (1) IP reputation & ASN analysis, (2) TLS fingerprinting JA3/JA4, (3) browser-environment detection, (4) behavioral biometrics (mouse curves, click timing, scroll velocity — scripts move in 'mathematically perfect lines with constant velocity'), (5) CAPTCHA challenges, (6) ML anomaly detection computing a per-request 'human-likelihood score.' Mismatched/over-consistent signals get blocked more than a single 'headless' tell.

Stealth for the browser path: use playwright-extra + puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth (a.k.a. playwright-stealth) to mask headless tells; it REDUCES but does not eliminate CAPTCHAs. With no paid CAPTCHA solver, the free strategy is avoidance: low request rate, realistic headers (consistent sec-ch-ua / Accept-Language for Egypt), persisted cookies/sessions between runs, and backing off on challenge.

The firecrawl tool (firecrawl.dev, ~70k stars; available here as the 'firecrawl' skill/CLI and self-hostable, MIT core) is an AI-extraction layer that returns clean markdown/JSON and handles JS rendering. Good for fast prototyping and resilient '/extract' structured pulls, but for a high-volume RECURRING amazon.eg job its hosted API is a paid/rate-limited dependency; self-hosting it still needs its own browser+proxy infra. Use it for discovery/prototyping, not as the core free production engine.

SCHEDULING — BullMQ (TypeScript-first, Redis-backed, MIT): the recommended worker engine. Gives persistent jobs, automatic retry/backoff, concurrency control, repeatable jobs / 'Job Schedulers' for cron-like cadence, job flows (DAGs), and a monitoring dashboard (Bull Board). Best for reliability + horizontal scale; cost is the Redis dependency.

SCHEDULING — node-cron: simplest in-process cron-syntax scheduler, but has NO built-in monitoring/alerting — every failure is silent unless you catch+report, and it dies if the web app process restarts. Acceptable only for tiny/non-critical jobs; do NOT run scraping inside the web app process.

SCHEDULING — Supabase Cron (pg_cron): schedule recurring jobs directly in Postgres; can call Database Functions, Edge Functions, or HTTP webhooks. Limit: up to 32 concurrent jobs (each uses a DB connection). Ideal as the free TRIGGER if you already use Supabase — have pg_cron POST to your worker/Edge Function on a daily/weekly/monthly cadence.

SCHEDULING — GitHub Actions cron: FREE on public repos (unlimited minutes; ~2,000 min/month on private free tier). BUT minimum interval is every 5 minutes, execution is NOT guaranteed on time (delayed under load — avoid 'on the hour' '0 * * *'), so it's best-effort. Great zero-infra option for daily/weekly/monthly snapshots where a few minutes' drift is fine; not for time-critical runs.

Architectural rule echoed across 2026 sources: move scheduled work OUT of the web-app process into dedicated infra (BullMQ workers / a cron service / Edge Functions). Separation is worth the complexity when job correctness matters.

Snapshot cadence design: daily/weekly/monthly price-history is low-volume, which plays to the free strategy's strength (the Amazon deep-dive says DIY with curl_cffi is viable under ~100K req/month). Spread requests over time, randomize order and delays, and store each run as an immutable timestamped snapshot for the web app's price-history charts.

WORKER DESIGN (concrete, free stack):
1) Repo: Node 20 + TypeScript. Deps: crawlee, playwright (Chromium), playwright-extra + puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth, bullmq, ioredis, cheerio, plus a Postgres/Supabase client. (Python variant: scrapy + scrapy-playwright OR curl_cffi+BeautifulSoup; everything below maps over.)
2) Two crawler tiers in one Crawlee project: TIER A = CheerioCrawler hitting the raw HTML first (fast, cheap, no browser). If the needed fields (price/title/ASIN) are present in HTML, parse with Cheerio and stop. TIER B = PlaywrightCrawler (Chromium + stealth) only as fallback when Tier A returns missing fields or a CAPTCHA/'Robot Check' page. In Playwright, block images/fonts/CSS via request interception to cut bandwidth and speed up.
3) Anti-block config (all free): rotate a small pool of realistic desktop User-Agents with MATCHING sec-ch-ua/Accept-Language='ar-EG,en;q=0.9'; enable Crawlee SessionPool + persist cookies across runs (storage/key-value store) so you keep a 'warm' session; cap maxConcurrency low (e.g. 1-2) and add randomized 3-10s delays + jitter; set maxRequestRetries with exponential backoff; on CAPTCHA detection, mark session bad, back off, and reschedule rather than hammering. For the HTTP tier specifically, prefer a TLS-impersonating client (curl_cffi in Python, or curl-impersonate / the real browser in Node) to defeat JA3/JA4.
4) Input = list of ASINs/URLs to track. Crawlee RequestQueue dedupes and persists URLs so a crashed run resumes. Each successful parse -> normalize to {asin, locale, title, price_egp, currency, in_stock, rating, reviews_count, seller, scraped_at} -> upsert a product row AND insert an immutable price_snapshot row (timestamped) for history charts in the web app.
5) SCHEDULING (pick by host): (a) Self-hosted/VPS -> BullMQ repeatable job ('Job Scheduler') enqueues a 'scrape-batch' job daily/weekly/monthly; a BullMQ Worker (separate process, NOT the web server) drives Crawlee; add Bull Board for monitoring + retries/backoff. (b) Supabase-based -> pg_cron schedules an HTTP webhook/Edge Function that enqueues the batch (respect the 32-concurrent-job limit). (c) Zero-infra/free -> GitHub Actions cron ('schedule:' with e.g. '17 3 * * *' for ~03:17 UTC daily — avoid exact-hour; 5-min floor; expect drift) runs the scraper container and writes results to your DB via service key. Use cron expressions: daily '17 3 * * *', weekly '17 3 * * 1', monthly '17 3 1 * *'.
6) Resilience: wrap each ASIN in try/catch, never let one failure kill the batch; log block-rate; alert on success-rate drop (node-cron/BullMQ won't alert by default — wire your own). Keep volume low (daily/weekly) to stay under Amazon's radar and within free limits.
RECOMMENDATION SUMMARY: Crawlee (Cheerio-first, Playwright+stealth fallback) + BullMQ/Redis workers for a real host, OR Crawlee + GitHub Actions cron if you want truly zero infrastructure for daily/weekly/monthly snapshots.

researchDimensions.topic: Defensible "most-selling / rising / estimated-demand" metrics from FREE scraped data (BSR snapshots + autocomplete) for Amazon Egypt (amazon.eg)
researchDimensions.summary: On a no-paid-API budget, the two scrapable signals that carry real demand information on amazon.eg are (1) Best Sellers Rank (BSR), shown per-product and on the live /gp/bestsellers and /gp/movers-and-shakers list pages, and (2) search autocomplete suggestions from Amazon's completion API. BSR is a relative, category-specific popularity rank (lower = more recent unit velocity, recalculated ~hourly); converting it to absolute units requires a category-calibrated power-law (Daily Sales ≈ A·BSR^B) that is only roughly accurate and that you CANNOT calibrate properly for Egypt without ground-truth, so treat BSR primarily as an ordinal rank, not a unit count. "Rising" is best derived yourself by snapshotting BSR over time and computing rank-velocity (the same logic Amazon's Movers & Shakers uses: percentage rank improvement vs ~24h ago), which needs no sales model and is the most defensible signal you have. "Estimated demand" for keywords should be a 0-100 score from autocomplete prefix-expansion (does the term surface, and how high in the list, across progressively longer prefixes) blended with the BSR of the products that term surfaces — never presented as a search-volume number. The whole product must visibly disclose that these are relative, modeled estimates with wide error bars, especially because amazon.eg is a thin marketplace where ranks are noisy.
keyFindings: BSR-to-sales is a power law: Daily Sales ≈ A × BSR^B. Published consumer-tool coefficients (Books, recalibrated Nov 2025): BSR 100-999 → A=31,622.78, B=-0.7781; BSR 1,000-99,999 → A=25,920, B=-0.778151; BSR 100,000+ → A=9,331.2, B=-0.778151. Sanity points: BSR #100 ≈ 1,000/day, #10,000 ≈ 20/day, #100,000 ≈ 1.2/day. These are BOOKS-specific and NOT valid for electronics/home — use only as a shape, not Egypt truth (bookbloom.io).

Category is the dominant error source: the SAME BSR of 100,000 ≈ 150-200 sales/mo in Books but only 30-40/mo in Home & Kitchen — a ~5x spread. There is no single cross-category formula; any sales number must be category-scoped, and you have no amazon.eg ground truth to fit B/A, so absolute unit claims for Egypt are 'Not verified' by construction.

Stated accuracy of even calibrated US/book models is ±10-15% at ranks 1-1,000, ±15-20% at 1k-10k, ±20-25% at 10k-100k, and worse beyond — and that is WITH proprietary calibration data you won't have for Egypt. Treat any displayed unit estimate as an order-of-magnitude band, not a point value (amzprep.com, easyparser.com).

Amazon Movers & Shakers is computed as PERCENTAGE rank improvement vs ~24h ago, updated ~hourly, per category — e.g. rank moved 30→10 = 200% gain. It measures momentum/velocity, NOT absolute volume, so a 30/day product can outrank a 200/day product. This is exactly the 'rising' metric and you can reproduce it from your own BSR snapshots without any sales model (amazon.com/gp/movers-and-shakers).

amazon.eg exposes the same list endpoints as other marketplaces — VERIFIED live: Best Sellers at https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/bestsellers and Movers & Shakers at https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/movers-and-shakers (the /-/en/ segment serves the English locale; drop it for Arabic). Best Sellers = top ~100 per node over ~last 24-48h sales (refreshed hourly); each list is paginated 1-50 / 51-100.

Per-product BSR lives in the 'Product information' / 'Additional Information' table on the detail page under a 'Best Sellers Rank' label (Arabic: 'الأكثر مبيعًا'), typically with a primary department rank plus one or more sub-category ranks, each a clickable category link. Scrape ALL ranks (the deepest sub-category rank is the most comparable across similar items). Detail-page and list scraping on amazon.eg returns 503 to naive bots (confirmed) — you need realistic headers, cookies, an Egypt/region IP, and throttling.

Amazon autocomplete uses a public completion API. Canonical shape: https://completion.amazon.eg/api/2017/suggestions?prefix=...&alias=aps&mid=<EG_marketplace_id>&... returning JSON {alias, prefix, suffix, suggestions:[...], responseId, shuffled}. Each suggestion carries the keyword text (and sometimes type/refTag). It returns ~10 ordered suggestions; order is treated as a relevance/popularity proxy (position 1 = strongest). A wrong/missing mid yields an empty suggestions array (observed), so the Egypt marketplace id must be captured from a real browser session.

Autocomplete demand-scoring heuristic (open-source MrXavier/amazon-autocomplete-keyword-score): for a target phrase, query each successive prefix ('i','ip','iph',...) and find the first prefix at which the full phrase appears and its INDEX in the returned list. Score starts at 100, is apportioned by prefix length, and is reduced by suggestion position (full credit at top, ~50% mid-list, near-zero at bottom); if the phrase is the #1 suggestion at an early prefix, stop early = max score. Net: terms that surface early (short prefix) AND high (low index) score highest.

Seed expansion for breadth: take each seed (category name, brand, top product noun) and append a-z / 0-9 (and common Arabic letters for the ar locale) as suffixes, harvest all returned suggestions, dedupe, then recurse one level on the most frequent stems. Frequency = how many distinct seed+letter queries surface a given suggestion; this co-occurrence count is a defensible relative-popularity proxy (the 'demand frequency') WITHOUT any volume number.

Snapshot cadence drives every window: capture BSR at a FIXED hour daily (Amazon recalcs ~hourly, so same-time sampling removes intraday phase noise). Daily risers = Δ over 1 snapshot; weekly = 7-snapshot trend/slope; monthly = ~30-snapshot trend. To approximate Amazon's own hourly Movers & Shakers you'd need hourly captures, but 1-4×/day is a realistic free-tier compromise. Keep a rolling 90-day history for trend/seasonality and to compute medians that suppress single-snapshot spikes.

Rank velocity is more robust than modeled units: rank improvement % over 24h = (BSR_prev − BSR_now)/BSR_prev. Because BSR is heavy-tailed, ALWAYS smooth in log space (use Δlog(BSR) = ln(BSR_prev) − ln(BSR_now)) and rank risers by that; a positive Δlog means improving. This is the single most defensible 'rising' metric and mirrors M&S without claiming unit counts.

amazon.eg is a comparatively THIN marketplace: many sub-categories have few competing ASINs, so BSR is volatile and a handful of sales can swing rank dramatically. This AMPLIFIES uncertainty vs amazon.com — small-sample noise must be disclosed, low-data categories flagged, and single-snapshot 'spikes' down-weighted vs sustained multi-day trends.

Free-stack architecture that works: persist (asin, category_node, bsr, captured_at, price_egp) snapshots in a time-series/relational store; derive list rank from /gp/bestsellers, momentum from /gp/movers-and-shakers + your own Δlog(BSR), and keyword demand from completion-API scores. Libraries: requests/httpx + rotating realistic UA/headers for static HTML, Playwright/Firecrawl only for JS/anti-bot pages, parsing with selectolax/lxml. Respect robots/ToS and rate-limit — this is scraping, not an API entitlement.
researchDimensions.egyptSpecifics: VERIFIED live on amazon.eg: Best Sellers at https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/bestsellers and Movers & Shakers at https://www.amazon.eg/-/en/gp/movers-and-shakers (the /-/en/ path = English locale; remove it for the default Arabic locale). Both mirror the standard Amazon list structure (top ~100 per category node, paginated 50/page, ~hourly refresh). Per-product BSR appears in the detail-page Product Information table under 'Best Sellers Rank' / Arabic 'الأكثر مبيعًا', usually a primary department rank plus sub-category ranks as category links; prices are in EGP. The autocomplete completion host is completion.amazon.eg with the 2017/suggestions JSON contract, but the correct Egypt marketplace id (mid) MUST be lifted from a live browser session — an absent/incorrect mid returns an empty suggestions array (observed). Practical caveat (confirmed): naive bot requests to amazon.eg list/detail pages return HTTP 503, so you need realistic headers/cookies, an Egypt-region IP, and throttling. NOT verified for Egypt: any BSR→unit-sales coefficients (all published A/B values are US/Books), category sales-velocity multipliers for the EG catalog, and absolute autocomplete search volumes — none can be calibrated without amazon.eg ground-truth sales, and the EG marketplace's thinner catalog makes ranks noisier than amazon.com.
researchDimensions.implementationNotes:
METRIC 1 — 'Most selling' (ordinal, most defensible): Scrape /gp/bestsellers per category node + per-product 'Best Sellers Rank' from detail pages. Rank items by ascending BSR WITHIN a category (never compare raw BSR across categories). Optionally show a 'sales band' (e.g. Very High / High / Moderard) by bucketing log(BSR) percentiles within that category from your own snapshot history — NOT a unit number. If you must show units, gate it behind a clearly-labeled 'rough estimate' using Daily≈A·BSR^B with category-specific A,B, and display it as a range (±50%+), not a figure.
METRIC 2 — 'Rising' (reproduce Movers & Shakers yourself): Snapshot BSR at a fixed hour. Riser score = Δlog(BSR) = ln(BSR_t-1) − ln(BSR_t) over the window (1 day / 7 day slope / 30 day slope). Equivalent %-gain (Amazon's M&S style) = (BSR_prev−BSR_now)/BSR_prev. Require a minimum prior BSR (e.g. exclude items entering from null/very deep ranks to avoid divide-by-noise) and require the gain to persist ≥2 snapshots for daily, or use the regression slope sign for weekly/monthly to suppress one-off spikes. Also surface Amazon's own /gp/movers-and-shakers list directly as a corroborating feed.
METRIC 3 — 'Estimated demand' for keywords: For each candidate phrase, hit completion.amazon.eg/api/2017/suggestions across its growing prefixes; KeywordScore = base 100, apportioned by the prefix length at which it first appears, multiplied by a position factor (1.0 at index 0 → ~0 at the list tail); early #1 appearance = max. Breadth via seed expansion: seed+([a-z0-9] and core Arabic letters) → harvest+dedupe suggestions → frequency = count of distinct seed-queries surfacing each suggestion. Final DemandScore (0-100) = 0.5·normalized_autocomplete_score + 0.3·normalized_inverse_median_BSR_of_top_matching_products + 0.2·normalized_riser_signal. Present ONLY as a 0-100 relative score with explicit 'no real search-volume' disclaimer.
CADENCE: BSR same-hour daily minimum; aim 2-4×/day if anti-bot budget allows for tighter daily risers; keep 90-day rolling history. Autocomplete: weekly full seed-expansion sweep + daily refresh of tracked terms.
UI UNCERTAINTY DISCLOSURE (required): (a) Label every sales number 'Estimated — modeled from public rank, not actual sales' with a visible ± range or a Low/Med/High confidence chip. (b) Show the underlying BSR and snapshot timestamp/freshness so users see the raw evidence. (c) For risers, plot the BSR sparkline (log axis) so a spike vs sustained trend is visually obvious; badge 'sustained' vs 'spike'. (d) Flag low-data categories ('few competing listings — rank is volatile'). (e) Keyword demand shown as a 0-100 score with tooltip 'relative interest from autocomplete, not search volume.' (f) Never rank cross-category by raw BSR; always scope or normalize. Treat any misleading 'X units sold' display as a Critical defect.
notVerified: Exact BSR→unit-sales coefficients for amazon.eg or for any non-Books category — all published A/B power-law values are US/Books-specific (Nov 2025 recalibration) and cannot be assumed valid for Egypt without local ground-truth sales.

The precise Egypt marketplace id (mid) for the completion API — must be captured from a live amazon.eg browser session; the test request returned an empty suggestions array, indicating mid/locale params were wrong.
Whether amazon.eg autocomplete suggestions are strictly ordered by search volume vs blended relevance/merch — order is used as a popularity PROXY only; Amazon does not document the ranking.

Real-world anti-bot tolerance / sustainable scrape rate for amazon.eg before blocking (only confirmed that naive requests return 503); proxy/IP and throttling requirements are inferred.
